claim: GIRK channels open and silence cellular electrical activity when inhibitory G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) are stimulated.
source: G protein gated inward rectifier K+ (GIRK) channels open and thereby silence cellular electrical activity when inhibitory G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) are stimulated.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general property of GIRK channels and is supported by established scientific knowledge about GIRK channel function.

claim: Four Gβγ subunits bind cooperatively to open GIRK2.
source: Using this assay we show that four Gβγ subunits bind cooperatively to open GIRK2
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the planar lipid bilayer assay and limiting slope analysis shown in the manuscript.

claim: Intracellular Na+ amplifies GIRK2 opening mostly by increasing Gβγ affinity.
source: intracellular Na+ – which enters neurons during action potentials – further amplifies opening mostly by increasing Gβγ affinity
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the effect of Na+ on Gβγ activation curves and the fitted cross-cooperativity factor.

claim: Intracellular Na+ enters neurons during action potentials.
source: intracellular Na+ – which enters neurons during action potentials
evidence: This is established knowledge about neuronal physiology.

claim: GIRK2 mediates a form of neuronal inhibition that is amplifiable in the setting of excess electrical activity through its dual responsiveness to Gβγ and Na+.
source: We conclude that GIRK2, through its dual responsiveness to Gβγ and Na+, mediates a form of neuronal inhibition that is amplifiable in the setting of excess electrical activity.
evidence: This conclusion is based on inference from the experimental data showing Na+ amplification and knowledge about Na+ entry during neuronal activity.

claim: Potassium channels oppose membrane electrical excitability by driving the membrane voltage towards the K+ reversal potential, near -90 mV in mammalian neurons.
source: Potassium channels oppose membrane electrical excitability by driving the membrane voltage towards the K+ reversal potential, near -90 mV in mammalian neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about potassium channel function and the K+ reversal potential in neurons.

claim: Many inhibitory neurotransmitters act through GPCRs which regulate GIRK channels.
source: In the nervous system many inhibitory neurotransmitters act through G protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), which regulate a G protein gated inward rectifier K+ (GIRK) channel (Pfaffinger et al., 1985; Lesage et al., 1994; Lesage et al., 1995; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Gβγ subunit binds to GIRK, favors the open conformation, and drives the membrane potential towards the K+ reversal potential.
source: A tight complex of the β and γ G protein subunits (known as the 'Gβγ subunit') binds to GIRK, favors the open conformation, and drives the membrane potential towards the K+ reversal potential (Pfaffinger et al., 1985; Logothetis et al., 1987; Reuveny et al., 1994; Krapivinsky et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies reported Gβγ affinity for GIRK channels in cell membranes ranging from 3 nM to 125 nM.
source: Furthermore, attempts to determine Gβγ affinity for GIRK channels in cell membranes, assessed by applying detergent-solubilized Gβγ to membrane patches, yielded values ranging from 3 nM to 125 nM (Wickman et al., 1994; Krapivinsky et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The membrane partition coefficient for detergent-solubilized Gβγ is not known.
source: The problem with these studies is the membrane partition coefficient for detergent-solubilized Gβγ is not known and therefore the membrane concentration is not known.
evidence: This is a critique of previous methods based on inference about their limitations.

claim: ITC measurements with soluble Gβγ and soluble cytoplasmic domain of GIRK measured the affinity to be 250 μM.
source: Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) measurements with a soluble form of Gβγ (lipid anchor-removed) and a soluble cytoplasmic domain of a GIRK channel (removed from the transmembrane pore) measured the affinity to be 250 μM (Yokogawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: ITC experiments can only report binding affinity in the absence of energetic coupling to a gated pore.
source: These experiments can only report binding affinity in the absence of energetic coupling to a gated pore, which was absent in the experiment.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the ITC method based on what was measured.

claim: Gβγ subunits and PIP2 are simultaneously required to open GIRK2 channels.
source: Using planar lipid bilayers in which purified GIRK2 channels, G protein subunits and PIP2 were reconstituted, we found that Gβγ subunits and PIP2 are simultaneously required to open GIRK2 channels (each alone is insufficient)
evidence: This is supported by data from previous reconstitution studies by the authors.

claim: Na+ is not required for GIRK2 channel opening, but modulates GIRK2 channel opening.
source: we found that Gβγ subunits and PIP2 are simultaneously required to open GIRK2 channels (each alone is insufficient) and that Na+ is not required for opening, but modulates GIRK2 channel opening.
evidence: This is supported by data from previous reconstitution studies by the authors.

claim: In the absence of Ni-NTA lipid, addition of 2 μM sGβγ-His10 failed to activate the channel.
source: In the absence of Ni-NTA lipid, addition of soluble Gβγ with a His-10 tag (sGβγ-His10) to a solution concentration of 2 μM failed to activate the channel.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When 2 μM sGβγ-His10 was added to a membrane formed with 0.0019 mol fraction Ni-NTA, channels were activated to about 60% of maximal activation.
source: In another experiment, when the same concentration of sGβγ-His10 was added to a membrane formed with 0.0019 mol fraction Ni-NTA (19 out of 10,000 lipid molecules in the membrane containing the Ni-NTA head group), channels were activated (Figure 1C). Subsequent addition of excess lipid-anchored Gβγ to the same membrane showed that about 60% of the GIRK channels had been activated by the Ni-NTA lipid-anchored Gβγ.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: sGβγ-His10 binds to Ni-NTA lipid with a Kd of 150 nM.
source: The curve is a rectangular hyperbola (binding isotherm) with a Kd of 150 nM (Figure 2C, black curve).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and curve fitting shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Fluorescent sGβγ-His10 binds to GUVs containing Ni-NTA lipid with an apparent dissociation constant around 90 nM.
source: A similar binding curve and affinity were determined for fluorescent sGβγ-His10 adsorption onto giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) containing Ni-NTA lipid at a mole fraction of 0.03 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: sGβγ-His4 binds to a single Ni-NTA lipid.
source: This result follows if sGβγ-His4 binds to a single Ni-NTA lipid and sGβγ-His10 binds to 3 Ni-NTA lipids.
evidence: This is inferred from the stoichiometric difference observed in the binding data.

claim: sGβγ-His10 binds to 3 Ni-NTA lipids.
source: This result follows if sGβγ-His4 binds to a single Ni-NTA lipid and sGβγ-His10 binds to 3 Ni-NTA lipids.
evidence: This is inferred from the stoichiometric difference observed in the binding data.

claim: A single Ni-NTA group is coordinated by 2 histidine residues separated by at least one histidine residue.
source: This stoichiometric difference is consistent with known structures of Ni-NTA-polyhistidine complexes, which show that a single Ni-NTA group is coordinated by 2 histidine residues separated by at least one histidine residue (Knecht et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural studies.

claim: At each Na+ concentration, normalized current increases as a steep sigmoidal function of membrane Gβγ concentration.
source: At each Na+ concentration, normalized current increases as a steep sigmoidal function of membrane Gβγ concentration (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The slope of Gβγ activation curves on a log-log plot at sufficiently low Gβγ concentrations are consistent with four Gβγ subunits being required to open a GIRK2 channel.
source: The slope of these functions on a log-log plot at sufficiently low Gβγ concentrations (achieved in these experiments for the Gβγ titrations at lower Na+ concentrations) are consistent with four Gβγ subunits being required to open a GIRK2 channel (see methods) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and limiting slope analysis shown in Figure 3C and the methods section.

claim: Gβγ activates the channel to a greater extent, especially at lower Gβγ concentrations, as Na+ is increased.
source: The titrations show that Gβγ activates the channel to a greater extent, especially at lower Gβγ concentrations, as Na+ is increased (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A tetramer GIRK2 channel has 4 structurally identical Gβγ binding sites and 4 Na+ binding sites.
source: This model was guided by atomic structures, which show that a tetramer GIRK2 channel has 4 structurally identical Gβγ binding sites and 4 Na+ binding sites (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural studies.

claim: All four Gβγ binding sites must be occupied on the channel before it opens.
source: First, all four Gβγ binding sites must be occupied on the channel before it opens, consistent with the limiting slope analysis (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the equilibrium model fitting to experimental data and limiting slope analysis.

claim: Gβγ binding is cooperative with a factor of 0.30, which means the fourth Gβγ subunit binds with an affinity 37 times higher than the first.
source: Second, Gβγ binding is cooperative with a factor of 0.30, which means the fourth Gβγ subunit binds with an affinity 37 times higher than the first.
evidence: This is supported by fitting the equilibrium model to experimental data.

claim: Gβγ binds with a Na+ cross cooperativity factor (η) of 0.63, which means Gβγ binds with 6-fold higher affinity when four Na+ sites are occupied compared to when the Na+ sites are not occupied.
source: Third, Gβγ binds with a Na+ cross cooperativity factor (η) of 0.63, which means Gβγ binds with 6-fold higher affinity when four Na+ sites are occupied compared to when the Na+ sites are not occupied.
evidence: This is supported by fitting the equilibrium model to experimental data.

claim: The effect of Na+ on Gβγ affinity accounts for channel opening at lower membrane Gβγ concentrations as Na+ concentration increases.
source: This effect of Na+ on Gβγ affinity accounts for channel opening at lower membrane Gβγ concentrations as Na+ concentration increases (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the model and experimental data.

claim: The strong cooperative binding of four Gβγ subunits accounts for the steep sigmoidal dependence of GIRK current on membrane Gβγ concentration.
source: The strong cooperative binding of four Gβγ subunits accounts for the steep sigmoidal dependence of GIRK current on membrane Gβγ concentration (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the model and experimental data.

claim: The Gβγ equilibrium constant decreases (i.e. the affinity for Gβγ increases) as Na+ concentration increases according to a rectangular hyperbola, with a ~6-fold difference between maximum and minimum values.
source: The Gβγ equilibrium constant decreases (i.e. the affinity for Gβγ increases) as Na+ concentration increases according to a rectangular hyperbola, with a ~6-fold difference between maximum and minimum values (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and curve fitting shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The apparent equilibrium constant for the effect of Na+ on Gβγ activation is ~5 mM.
source: The apparent equilibrium constant for the effect of Na+ on Gβγ activation is ~5 mM, which is very close to the physiological Na+ concentration in the cytoplasm of a resting neuron (Rose and Ransom, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data fitting shown in Figure 4B and citation to literature about physiological Na+ concentration.

claim: The physiological Na+ concentration in the cytoplasm of a resting neuron is close to 5 mM.
source: The apparent equilibrium constant for the effect of Na+ on Gβγ activation is ~5 mM, which is very close to the physiological Na+ concentration in the cytoplasm of a resting neuron (Rose and Ransom, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The GIRK2 channel's response to Gβγ should be sensitive to changes in Na+ concentration right in the physiological range.
source: Thus, the GIRK2 channel's response to Gβγ should be sensitive to changes in Na+ concentration right in the physiological range.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured Na+ Kd being close to physiological Na+ concentration.

claim: When four Gβγ subunits bind to the cytoplasmic domain of GIRK2, they cause the ring to rotate as a rigid body with respect to the pore, which twists open the helical bundle that forms the pore's gate.
source: When four Gβγ subunits bind to the cytoplasmic domain of GIRK2, which forms a ring made by the four channel subunits, they cause the ring to rotate as a rigid body with respect to the pore, which twists open the helical bundle that forms the pore's gate (Whorton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural studies.

claim: Because the rigid body rotation involves all four subunits at once, conformational changes induced by the binding of Gβγ to one site will favor binding at the neighboring sites (i.e. positive cooperativity).
source: Because the rigid body rotation involves all four subunits at once, conformational changes induced by the binding of Gβγ to one site will favor binding at the neighboring sites (i.e. positive cooperativity).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural mechanism and experimental cooperativity data.

claim: Gβγ binds more favorably to the channel's open conformation.
source: A cartoon illustrating this concept depicts Gβγ binding more favorably to the channel's open conformation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural mechanism and cooperativity data.

claim: Because opening involves a concerted rotation of the subunits, all four Gβγ binding sites change to higher affinity at once, giving rise to strong positive cooperativity.
source: Because opening involves a concerted rotation of the subunits, all four Gβγ binding sites change to higher affinity at once, giving rise to strong positive cooperativity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural mechanism and cooperativity data.

claim: At the highest (0.03) Ni-NTA lipid mole fraction Na+ increases current approximately 2.5-fold when Na+ is increased from 0 mM to 32 mM.
source: In addition to increasing Gβγ affinity, Na+ also increases the GIRK2 current when the Gβγ binding sites are fully occupied: at the highest (0.03) Ni-NTA lipid mole fraction Na+ increases current approximately 2.5-fold when Na+ is increased from 0 mM to 32 mM (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The increase in GIRK2 current with Na+ at saturating Gβγ follows a rectangular hyperbola.
source: This increase follows a rectangular hyperbola.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data fitting.

claim: Na+ stabilizes the open, conductive state of the channel in direct proportion to its occupancy on the channel.
source: The simplest physical explanation for this behavior, which is also consistent with the equilibrium model, is that Na+ stabilizes the open, conductive state of the channel in direct proportion to its occupancy on the channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model and experimental data.

claim: Four Gβγ subunits bind to GIRK2 and permit opening to a probability that is higher in proportion to occupancy of the Na+ sites.
source: In other words, four Gβγ subunits bind to GIRK2 and permit opening to a probability that is higher in proportion to occupancy of the Na+ sites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model and experimental data.

claim: By thermodynamic linkage, Na+ would increase the apparent affinity of Gβγ for GIRK2 and it would also increase the maximum level of current reached when four Gβγ subunits bind.
source: Thus, by thermodynamic linkage, Na+ would increase the apparent affinity of Gβγ for GIRK2 and it would also increase the maximum level of current reached when four Gβγ subunits bind.
evidence: This is an inference based on thermodynamic principles and the model.

claim: The Na+ binding sites are located at the interface between the cytoplasmic domains and the transmembrane pore, where opening is transduced through the binding of Gβγ.
source: This physical mechanism is consistent with the location of the Na+ binding sites at the interface between the cytoplasmic domains and the transmembrane pore, where opening is transduced through the binding of Gβγ (Figure 5A) (Whorton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural studies.

claim: Na+ in the absence of Gβγ does not open GIRK.
source: It is also consistent with the observations that Na+ in the absence of Gβγ does not open GIRK (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In crystal structures Na+ binds to GIRK but does not cause a rotation of the cytoplasmic domain in the absence of Gβγ.
source: in crystal structures Na+ binds to GIRK but does not cause a rotation of the cytoplasmic domain in the absence of Gβγ (Whorton and MacKinnon, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous structural studies.

claim: Na+ facilitates Gβγ-mediated pore opening.
source: Thus, Na+ facilitates Gβγ-mediated pore opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and functional data.

claim: GIRK2 suppresses electrical activity in neurons when inhibitory neurotransmitters stimulate GPCRs on the cell surface, such as GABAB receptors.
source: GIRK2 suppresses electrical activity in neurons when inhibitory neurotransmitters stimulate GPCRs on the cell surface, such as GABAB receptors, which release Gβγ on the intracellular membrane surface to open GIRK2 channels.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GIRK2 function in neurons.

claim: The level of GIRK2 channel opening brought about by released Gβγ potentially depends on the intracellular Na+ concentration.
source: At the same time, the level of GIRK2 channel opening – and therefore the level of neuronal inhibition – brought about by the released Gβγ potentially depends on the intracellular Na+ concentration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing Na+ amplification.

claim: At all Gβγ concentrations, the level of GIRK2 current is increased as Na+ is increased.
source: This conclusion derives from the family of Gβγ activation curves (Figure 3B): at all Gβγ concentrations, the level of GIRK2 current is increased as Na+ is increased.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At high Gβγ concentrations amplification is 2.5-fold when Na+ is increased from 0 to 32 mM, while at lower Gβγ concentrations amplification approaches ten fold.
source: Na+-amplification is clearly not constant but is instead a function of the Gβγ concentration: at high Gβγ concentrations (right side of graph) amplification is 2.5-fold (i.e. GIRK2 current increases 2.5-fold) when Na+ is increased from 0 to 32 mM, while at lower Gβγ concentrations (corresponding to the steep sigmoidal rise in current) amplification approaches ten fold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cytosolic Na+ increases with higher levels of electrical activity due to Na+ entry through both synaptic channels and voltage-dependent Na+ channels.
source: The potential importance of Na+ amplification to neuronal electrical signaling lies in the fact that cytosolic Na+ increases with higher levels of electrical activity due to Na+ entry through both synaptic channels and voltage-dependent Na+ channels (Lasser-Ross and Ross, 1992; Fleidervish et al., 2010, Rose and Konnerth, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Na+ amplification should provide a mechanism for strengthening an inhibitory input to a more active neuron.
source: Thus, Na+ amplification should, in principle, provide a mechanism for strengthening an inhibitory input to a more active neuron.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and knowledge about Na+ entry during neuronal activity.

claim: Baclofen-activated currents had the strongly inwardly-rectifying current-voltage relationship expected from GIRK channel activation.
source: Baclofen-activated currents had the strongly inwardly-rectifying current-voltage relationship expected from GIRK channel activation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Baclofen-activated GIRK current was much smaller in neurons recorded with 0 mM internal Na+ compared with those recorded with 27 mM internal Na+.
source: Baclofen-activated GIRK current was much smaller in neurons recorded with 0 mM internal Na+ compared with those recorded with 27 mM internal Na+ (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Currents measured with 27 mM internal Na+ were amplified by an average of 8 fold compared to currents with 0 mM Na+.
source: Currents measured with 27 mM internal Na+ were amplified by an average of 8 fold compared to currents with 0 mM Na+.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: From the Gβγ/Na+ titration data, 8-fold amplification corresponds to a Gβγ concentration of about 0.003 in NTA-lipid mole fraction units.
source: From the Gβγ/Na+ titration data (Figure 3B), 8-fold amplification corresponds to a Gβγ concentration of about 0.003 in NTA-lipid mole fraction units (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the amplification curve derived from experimental data.

claim: In the concentration range around 0.003 NTA-lipid mole fraction the amplification curve becomes very steep, allowing relatively small cell-to-cell variations in Gβγ concentration to translate into larger differences in current response.
source: In this concentration range the amplification curve becomes very steep, allowing relatively small cell-to-cell variations in Gβγ concentration to translate into larger differences in current response (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the shape of the amplification curve.

claim: The steep amplification curve offers an explanation for the large spread of current values measured upon baclofen activation in the presence of 27 mM Na+.
source: This property offers an explanation for the large spread of current values measured upon baclofen activation in the presence of 27 mM Na+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the steep amplification curve and experimental variability.

claim: The estimated Gβγ concentration stimulated by baclofen in dopamine neurons is centered in the middle of the steep sigmoidal rising phase of the Gβγ-activation curves.
source: Most importantly, the estimated Gβγ concentration stimulated by baclofen in dopamine neurons (Figure 6D,E) is centered in the middle of the steep sigmoidal rising phase of the Gβγ-activation curves (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the estimated Gβγ concentration to the activation curves.

claim: In the regime where Gβγ concentration is in the middle of the steep sigmoidal rising phase, even modest changes in intracellular Na+ concentration should amplify Gβγ-mediated inhibition of neuronal electrical activity.
source: In this regime even modest changes in intracellular Na+ concentration should amplify Gβγ-mediated inhibition of neuronal electrical activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the position of physiological Gβγ concentration on the activation curves.

claim: Intracellular Na+ in dendrites can double during synaptic activity.
source: Intracellular Na+ in dendrites can double during synaptic activity (Rose and Konnerth, 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: High local increases in Na+ occur in cell bodies and axons during action potential firing.
source: high local increases also occur in cell bodies and axons during action potential firing (Lasser-Ross and Ross, 1992; Fleidervish et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Na+ amplification of GIRK currents likely occurs during normal physiological activity.
source: Thus, the Na+ amplification of GIRK currents likely occurs during normal physiological activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on knowledge about Na+ changes during neuronal activity.

claim: During epileptiform activity, intracellular Na+ can likely reach 30 mM.
source: Even stronger amplification is likely during epileptiform activity, when intracellular Na+ can likely reach 30 mM (Raimondo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A mole fraction value 0.003 translates into approximately 1200 Gβγ subunits per μm2 of membrane.
source: Taking into account the surface area of a lipid head group and the stoichiometry of 3 Ni-NTA lipid molecules per sGβγ-His10 subunit, a mole fraction value 0.003 (i.e. the concentration of Gβγ subunits estimated in dopamine neurons) translates into approximately 1200 Gβγ subunits per μm2 of membrane.
evidence: This is a calculation based on known lipid properties and experimental stoichiometry.

claim: 1200 Gβγ subunits per μm2 of membrane corresponds to approximately 280 μM Gβγ concentration in the solution layer adjacent to the membrane.
source: To place this 2-dimensional membrane density into more familiar concentration units we multiply the membrane surface area by the linear dimension of a Gβγ subunit (about 70 Å) to approximate a Gβγ concentration in the solution layer adjacent to the membrane equal to 280 μM.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the membrane density and Gβγ dimensions.

claim: At 280 μM Gβγ concentration GIRK is between 10% and 80% activated, depending on the Na+ concentration.
source: At this Gβγ concentration GIRK is between 10% and 80% activated, depending on the Na+ concentration (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on reading values from the experimental activation curves.

claim: The apparent affinity of Gβγ for the GIRK channel is in the range of 280 μM.
source: Thus, the apparent affinity of Gβγ for the GIRK channel is in this range.
evidence: This is an inference based on the estimated Gβγ concentration and activation level.

claim: The estimated apparent affinity of 280 μM is close to the affinity reported using ITC (250 μM).
source: This estimate is close to the affinity reported using ITC to study the interaction of lipid anchor-removed Gβγ in solution with the soluble cytoplasmic domain of a GIRK channel (250 μM) (Yokogawa et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison to previously published data.

claim: The cytoplasmic domain removed from the pore binds to Gβγ according to a 1:1 binding isotherm.
source: Removed from the pore, the cytoplasmic domain, even though it is a tetramer with four Gβγ binding sites like the full channel, binds to Gβγ according to a 1:1 binding isotherm.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous ITC studies.

claim: The first Gβγ subunit binds to the full GIRK2 channel with an equilibrium constant of 0.019 mol fraction corresponding to 1.9 mM in the solution layer adjacent to the membrane.
source: As we have shown here, the full GIRK2 channel by contrast exhibits strong cooperativity, the first Gβγ subunit binding with very low affinity (equilibrium constant 0.019 mol fraction corresponding to 1.9 mM in the solution layer adjacent to the membrane)
evidence: This is based on the fitted cooperativity model parameters.

claim: The fourth Gβγ subunit binds to the full GIRK2 channel with an equilibrium constant of (0.019) × (0.3)^3 mol fraction corresponding to 50 μM in the solution layer adjacent to the membrane.
source: the fourth binding with higher affinity (equilibrium constant (0.019) × (0.3)3 mol fraction corresponding to 50 μM in the solution layer adjacent to the membrane).
evidence: This is based on the fitted cooperativity model parameters.

claim: The cooperativity that gives rise to the steep dependence of GIRK channel activity on Gβγ concentration is completely lost when the transmembrane pore is removed.
source: This cooperativity, which gives rise to the steep dependence of GIRK channel activity on Gβγ concentration, is completely lost when the transmembrane pore is removed.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the full channel behavior to the isolated cytoplasmic domain.

claim: When the pore is removed, Gβγ binding free energy is no longer utilized to twist open the pore's helical gate, and at the same time the rotational origin of cooperativity disappears.
source: The mechanism proposed for coupling Gβγ binding to pore opening, illustrated in Figure 5, offers an explanation: when the pore is removed, Gβγ binding free energy is no longer utilized to twist open the pore's helical gate, and at the same time the rotational origin of cooperativity disappears.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural mechanism.

claim: The ITC-determined affinity of 250 μM lies in between the affinities of the first (1.9 mM) and fourth (50 μM) Gβγ subunits to bind to the intact, cooperative system.
source: The ITC-determined affinity of 250 μM lies in between the affinities of the first (1.9 mM) and fourth (50 μM) Gβγ subunits to bind to the intact, cooperative system.
evidence: This is a comparison of the ITC affinity to the calculated affinities from the cooperative model.

claim: The interaction of Gβγ with GIRK2 is weak compared to other known protein complexes.
source: In the context of other known protein complexes, the interaction of Gβγ with GIRK2 is weak, consistent with a short lifetime for the complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured affinity values.

claim: Two proteins with a diffusion-limited association rate constant of 10^7 M^-1sec^-1 will remain in complex on average for less than 2 milliseconds if the equilibrium constant is 50 μM.
source: For example, two proteins with a diffusion-limited association rate constant of, say, 107 M-1sec-1, will remain in complex on average for less than 2 milliseconds if the equilibrium constant is 50 μM (i.e. affinity of the fourth Gβγ subunit)
evidence: This is a calculation based on kinetic principles.

claim: The lifetime of an activated channel (GIRK2 with 4 Gβγ subunits) is less than 0.5 milliseconds.
source: the lifetime of an activated channel (GIRK2 with 4 Gβγ subunits, any one of which can dissociate) less than 0.5 milliseconds.
evidence: This is a calculation based on kinetic principles and the four binding sites.

claim: The lifetime of an active channel will be brief compared to the duration of macroscopic GIRK current in a cell during GPCR stimulation (~1 s).
source: Even if the association rate constant is smaller, the lifetime of an active channel will be brief compared to the duration of macroscopic GIRK current in a cell during GPCR stimulation (~1 s) (Ford et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the calculated lifetime and citation to literature about GIRK current duration.

claim: Gβγ apparently associates and dissociates many times on and off the channel during a period of stimulation.
source: This means Gβγ apparently associates and dissociates many times on and off the channel during a period of stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the brief lifetime to the duration of stimulation.

claim: Gβγ binds to Gα(GDP) with greater than ten thousand times higher affinity (Kd ~1 nM) than to the channel.
source: Because Gβγ binds to Gα(GDP) with greater than ten thousand times higher affinity (Kd ~1 nM Sarvazyan et al., 1998) than to the channel
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Whenever Gα(GTP) hydrolyses GTP to GDP it will rapidly bind free Gβγ and remove it from the channel by mass action.
source: whenever Gα(GTP) hydrolyses GTP to GDP it will rapidly bind free Gβγ and remove it from the channel by mass action.
evidence: This is an inference based on the much higher affinity of Gβγ for Gα(GDP).

claim: The very weak binding of Gβγ to the channel means that the duration of GIRK current activation during GPCR stimulation will be controlled by the lifetime of Gα(GTP).
source: Thus, the very weak binding of Gβγ to the channel means that the duration of GIRK current activation during GPCR stimulation will be controlled by the lifetime of Gα(GTP).
evidence: This is an inference based on the weak Gβγ-GIRK affinity and strong Gβγ-Gα(GDP) affinity.

claim: The Gβγ concentrations reported represent the thermodynamic activity concentrations in equilibrium with the GIRK channel.
source: The Gβγ concentrations reported here represent the thermodynamic activity concentrations in equilibrium with the GIRK channel.
evidence: This is a clarification about what the measured concentrations represent.

claim: In living cells it is distinctly possible that GIRK and GPCRs/G proteins reside in specialized regions of the cell membrane.
source: In living cells it is distinctly possible that GIRK and GPCRs/G proteins reside in specialized regions of the cell membrane.
evidence: This is speculation about the organization of proteins in cell membranes.

claim: If GIRK and GPCRs/G proteins reside in specialized regions, the relevant density of Gβγ is the local density near GIRK channels, which would be much higher than that averaged over the entire membrane.
source: In this case the relevant density of Gβγ is the local density near GIRK channels, which would be much higher than that averaged over the entire membrane.
evidence: This is speculation about local Gβγ concentrations if proteins are organized in specialized regions.
